content.text: Content goes live on every commit, without a rebuild. When an editor publishes, Alinea commits the change to your repository and your site starts serving it right away.

Every publish in the dashboard is a git commit. After the commit, the site syncs the new content sha from its own handler, so the next request that renders content reads the latest version. No build or redeploy has to finish before editors see their changes on the live site.

Only set this up once your deployed site has a backend that syncs content at runtime: Alinea Cloud or a self-hosted backend. Without one, a deployment is how new content reaches your site, so skipping content-only builds would leave published changes offline.

Because content is synced at runtime, a commit that only changes content does not need a new deployment. On Vercel you can skip those builds with an `ignoreCommand` in `vercel.json`. The command exits successfully, which tells Vercel to skip the build, when nothing outside the `content` directory changed since the last deployment that built:

`VERCEL_GIT_PREVIOUS_SHA` is the commit of the last deployment that built, so the comparison covers every commit pushed since, not only the last one. Vercel clones only the last 10 commits, though, and once content commits skip their builds, the last build soon lies further back than that. When its commit is missing from the clone, or on the first deployment of a branch, the command compares against the previous commit instead. Comparing against a missing commit would fail, and a failing command builds, so every content commit would quietly be built again.
Adjust `content` if your content lives in a different directory.

A skipped build shows as Canceled in the deployments of your Vercel project, and the list hides canceled deployments by default. Filter on Status → Canceled to find them: their log ends with "Ignored Build Step command returned exit code 0". To check the whole setup:
Publish a change in the dashboard.
Find the deployment of its commit: it shows as Canceled.
Load the page: it shows the change without a redeploy.
This checks both halves of the setup: content-only commits skip their build, and the site syncs their content at runtime.

Static pages are revalidated for you. Every page that queries content is tagged, and after each commit the handler marks those pages as stale. The next visit is still answered from the cache while Next.js rebuilds the page in the background, and the visit after that gets the new content. No visitor waits for a render, and no `revalidatePath` call is needed. This includes pages generated with `generateStaticParams`: revalidation code in `afterCommit` that refreshes them by hand, such as `revalidateTag('_N_T_/layout')` or `revalidatePath('/', 'layout')`, can be removed.

Pages rendered at request time sync on their next render. The first one after a commit can still show the previous version while the shared content sha refreshes. Content pushed to your repository without the dashboard, for example a local edit, skips the handler: pages pick it up within five minutes, or within `syncInterval` seconds when your config sets it. Use the handler's `afterCommit` hook if other caches in your app depend on content, for example your own `fetch` tags.
